Grounding reconnects attention with the present. It can provide temporary steadiness, but it does not solve the underlying problem. Afterward, the issue may still need attention; grounding works best as a bridge to the next useful step rather than automatic avoidance.

## Ways to ground {#ways-to-ground}

### Tactile

Feel the feet against the floor, the body supported by a chair, the texture of fabric, or a familiar object in the hand. Notice safe changes in temperature without using pain or extreme cold.

### Sensory

Name what sight, sound, smell, taste, and touch are noticing. Describe the room in concrete detail. Orient to your location, the date, the approximate time, and what is happening now.

### Cognitive

Count, name items in a category, spell a word, or state simple orienting facts. Use a task that is engaging enough to reconnect attention without becoming another source of pressure.

### Imagery

Picture a steadying place or recall the realistic words of a supportive person. Imagery should support orientation, not require pretending that the current problem is gone.

### Social

Contact a supportive person, spend time with a pet, read a supportive message, use humour where it fits, or do something small and meaningful for another person.

### Body scan

Move attention gradually through the body. Notice contact, tension, ease, temperature, or numbness without rushing and without forcing change.

### Movement

Movement helps some people reconnect with the present. Choose movement that is safe for your health and ability. [TIPP and Intense Exercise](/learn/distress-tolerance/tipp.html#intense-exercise) include separate suitability guidance.

## Breathing as an anchor {#breathing-anchor}

A comfortable breath can be one anchor among many. Do not force a pace or prescribe breath-holding. People respond differently: stop if you feel light-headed, distressed, or uncomfortable, and consult a health-care practitioner when a breathing practice may not be appropriate.

[Box Breathing](/tool-finder/box-breathing/) offers adjustable holds that can be set to zero. Choose another grounding anchor if breath focus is uncomfortable.

## Choose a next step {#next-step}

After grounding, ask: *What needs attention now?* The answer might be problem-solving, support, rest, a boundary, a safety step, or another skill.

[Open the Grounding tool](/tool-finder/grounding/) for a concise guided practice. [Positive Self-Talk](/tool-finder/positive-self-talk/) can help create a supportive phrase.
